clinicalPearls: Acute immune-mediated haemolytic reactions occur when recipient preformed antibodies lyse transfused donor RBCs, during or up to 24 h after transfusion; anti-A/anti-B antibodies cause most of the most severe (potentially fatal) reactions, though alloantibodies against Rh, Kell, and Duffy antigens can also cause severe haemolysis (Harrison 22e p.906).

The most dramatic acute haemolytic reactions are usually caused by a failure in product or patient identification, erroneous blood grouping, or unidentified recipient anti-RBC alloimmunisation - i.e. a clerical/identification error (Harrison 22e p.906).

Acute haemolytic reactions may present with hypotension, tachypnoea, tachycardia, fever (rise of 1-2 degrees C), chills, chest and back/flank pain, haemoglobinuria, and haemoglobinemia; in the most severe cases DIC, acute renal failure, shock, and death may occur (Harrison 22e p.906).

RED FLAG: when an adverse reaction is suspected the transfusion must be STOPPED, the recipient's clinical status assessed, and supportive care initiated; a thorough clerical check is crucial to prevent a possible second misidentified transfusion (Harrison 22e p.908).

Management of acute immune haemolytic reaction is mainly supportive: prompt interruption of transfusion, biological workup, vigorous isotonic saline hydration with diuretics to maintain urine output; may require forced alkaline diuresis, electrolyte correction, and pressor support, and in DIC with bleeding, platelet/plasma/cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen (Harrison 22e p.908).

Diagnosis of transfusion-associated haemolysis relies on persistent/worsening anaemia, depleted haptoglobin, haemoglobinemia and haemoglobinuria, and elevated LDH and unconjugated bilirubin; the direct antiglobulin test (DAT/direct Coombs) is most often positive, as is the indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) (Harrison 22e p.908).

Delayed haemolytic reactions present with icterus and persisting or worsening anaemia and result from an anamnestic response in previously sensitised patients who had a negative alloantibody screen at transfusion (low antibody levels); the alloantibody becomes detectable 1-2 weeks after transfusion (Harrison 22e p.906).

FNHTR (febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction) is the most frequent reaction to cellular components (up to 300 per 100,000), characterised by chills, rigors and a rise of at least 1 degree C, caused by proinflammatory cytokines in the component or recipient antibodies against donor antigens; it is a diagnosis of exclusion once infection and haemolysis are ruled out (Harrison 22e p.911).
Leukocyte reduction (especially prestorage) can prevent FNHTR; premedication with antipyretics has generally proven ineffective and may mask relevant clinical symptoms (Harrison 22e p.911).

Most allergic transfusion reactions are mild (rash, pruritus, urticaria, localised oedema) and relate to plasma proteins; rarely they are severe/anaphylactic with bronchospasm, respiratory distress, hypotension, nausea, vomiting and shock - anaphylaxis can occur after only a few millilitres of component (Harrison 22e p.911).

TRALI is characterised by occurrence or worsening of hypoxia and NONcardiogenic pulmonary oedema with bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray during or within 6 h of transfusion (delayed cases up to 72 h); it is among the most common causes of transfusion-related fatalities and treatment is supportive only (Harrison 22e p.911).

TRALI usually results from donor plasma containing high-titre anti-HLA class II antibodies binding recipient cognate antigen (anti-HLA class I and anti-HNA antibodies may also be involved); a cytokine/chemokine-mediated mechanism without HLA interaction can also occur (Harrison 22e p.911).

TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) is common and underrecognised and is now the main cause of transfusion-related death since TRALI risk was mitigated; it presents with dyspnoea, hypoxia, bilateral and predominantly ALVEOLAR infiltrates on chest x-ray, frequent systolic hypertension, and elevated BNP (fever may also occur) (Harrison 22e p.912).

TRALI vs TACO distinction: TRALI gives noncardiogenic oedema with predominantly interstitial infiltrates within 6 h, whereas TACO is volume overload with predominantly alveolar infiltrates (within 12 h), systolic hypertension and elevated BNP; TACO risk factors include older age, renal failure, preexisting fluid overload, cardiac dysfunction, large transfusion volume and excessive transfusion rate (Harrison 22e p.911-912).

Transfusion-related GVHD is extremely rare but fatal in over 90% of cases; mediated by engrafted donor T lymphocytes in a recipient unable to reject them, it presents 5-10 days post-transfusion with cytopenia, fever, characteristic skin rash, diarrhoea and liver function abnormalities, and is prevented by irradiation (minimum 25 Gy) of cellular components in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.911).

Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection remains a significant concern, notably with platelet concentrates stored at room temperature; some gram-negatives such as Yersinia grow at 4 degrees C and can contaminate RBC units - recipients may develop abrupt fever and chills deteriorating to septic shock, DIC and death, and after culture sampling broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started promptly (Harrison 22e p.913).

Iron overload: each RBC concentrate contains 200-250 mg of iron; in frequently transfused recipients untreated accumulation impairs endocrine, hepatic and cardiac function (death may occur from cardiac failure or arrhythmia), assessed by serum ferritin, MRI and liver biopsy, and prevented/treated by monitoring and iron chelation (Harrison 22e p.912).

Acute hypotensive transfusion reactions are an abrupt drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 30 mmHg early after starting transfusion that resolves once transfusion is stopped; they are more likely in patients taking ACE inhibitors (impaired bradykinin metabolism) and the same product should NOT be restarted (Harrison 22e p.912).
harrison.pathophysiology: Adverse reactions to blood components arise via immune or nonimmune mechanisms. Immune-mediated acute haemolysis occurs when recipient preformed antibodies (anti-A/anti-B IgM/IgG, or alloantibodies to Rh, Kell, Duffy) lyse transfused donor RBCs, with complement activation; ABO incompatibility classically results from clerical/identification error. Delayed haemolysis reflects an anamnestic alloantibody response (neoformed allogeneic IgG, C3b-mediated opsonisation and ADCC-mediated phagocytosis) detectable 1-2 weeks later. FNHTR is driven by proinflammatory cytokines accumulated in the component or recipient antibodies against donor leukocyte antigens. Allergic/anaphylactic reactions relate to plasma proteins and soluble mediators triggering histamine/serotonin release (IgA-deficient recipients may react to IgA). TRALI results from donor anti-HLA (class II, also class I) or anti-HNA antibodies binding recipient antigen, or cytokine/chemokine priming, causing neutrophil aggregation in pulmonary vasculature and release of inflammatory mediators producing noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema. TACO is hydrostatic circulatory overload from excessive volume/rate relative to cardiac/renal reserve. Transfusion-associated GVHD is mediated by engrafted donor T lymphocytes attacking host HLA antigens. (Harrison 22e p.906-912)

harrison.prognosis: Most adverse reactions are non-life-threatening, though serious reactions can present with mild symptoms. An average of ~37 transfusion-associated fatalities (possible-to-definite imputability) were reported yearly to the FDA between 2017-2021 among ~15 million transfused components, with leading causes of death being TACO (32%), TRALI (21%), haemolysis (21%) and microbial contamination (13%). Acute haemolysis is often self-limiting but can be fatal (DIC, acute renal failure, shock). Transfusion-associated GVHD is fatal in over 90% of cases and highly resistant to treatment. (Harrison 22e p.906-911)
pitfalls: Premedication with antipyretics for FNHTR is generally ineffective and may mask relevant clinical warning symptoms
FNHTR must not be diagnosed until infection and haemolysis are excluded
Failing to perform a clerical/identification check risks a second misidentified (incompatible) transfusion
TRALI and TACO are easily confused; both cause hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates - TACO is now the leading cause of transfusion death and is underrecognised
In acute hypotensive reactions the same blood product should not be restarted; consider switching ACE inhibitor for patients needing further transfusion
Delayed haemolytic reactions occur despite a negative pretransfusion alloantibody screen (low antibody levels) - icterus and worsening anaemia 1-2 weeks later
Iron overload is frequently underreported in chronically transfused patients
Further RBC transfusion in hyperhaemolytic reaction (sickle cell disease) typically exacerbates ongoing haemolysis
harrison.severityClassification: Warning-sign based recognition of transfusion adverse reactions (Harrison Table 118-5): fever of at least 38 degrees C (rise of 1-2 degrees C within 4 h favours FNHTR or TRALI; rise over 2 degrees C favours bacterial infection/haemolysis); hypotension (systolic drop of at least 30 mmHg) suggesting haemolytic, anaphylactic or septic shock; dyspnoea (TRALI within 6 h, TACO within 12 h, severe allergy within 4 h); haemoglobinuria (intravascular haemolysis); rash (minor allergy if under two-thirds body, severe if over two-thirds, anaphylaxis if with dyspnoea/shock within 5 min); icterus (delayed haemolysis); rash/diarrhoea/fever 2 days-6 weeks (GVHD); gum bleeding/purpura 5-12 days (posttransfusion purpura). Reactions are also categorised as immune-mediated vs nonimmunologic, and by timing (acute vs delayed). (Harrison 22e p.908)

management: Stop the transfusion immediately at any suspected reaction, maintain venous access, and perform a rigorous clerical and identity check to prevent a second misidentified transfusion
For acute haemolytic reactions give vigorous isotonic saline to maintain urine output with diuretics as needed, support blood pressure with vasopressors, and correct electrolytes
Manage haemolysis-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation with platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen when there is bleeding
Treat febrile non-haemolytic reactions with antipyretics after excluding haemolysis, and allergic reactions with antihistamines, escalating to adrenaline and corticosteroids for anaphylaxis
When bacterial contamination is suspected, culture the component and recipient and start broad-spectrum antibiotics
Send diagnostic samples including direct and indirect antiglobulin tests, repeat ABO grouping and crossmatch, and report to the transfusion service
Prevent recurrence with appropriate component selection using leucoreduced units, washed or IgA-deficient components for IgA-deficient recipients, and premedication where indicated
